questions.q: Before joining the United States, Vermont spent 14 years as what?
questions.explanation: Vermont declared independence in 1777 and governed itself as the Vermont Republic until statehood in 1791.

questions.q: Vermont became a U.S. state in 1791 as which number state?
questions.explanation: Vermont was the 14th state — the first admitted after the original thirteen colonies.

questions.q: Vermont's 1777 constitution was the first in America to do what?
questions.explanation: The 1777 constitution of the Vermont Republic was the first to abolish adult slavery and grant suffrage to men without property requirements.

questions.q: Which Revolutionary War hero led the Green Mountain Boys and helped capture Fort Ticonderoga in 1775?
questions.explanation: Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys (with Benedict Arnold along) seized Fort Ticonderoga on May 10, 1775.

questions.q: Ethan Allen's brother, who founded the University of Vermont and gave Burlington much of its early shape, was named what?
questions.explanation: Ira Allen is considered a founder of Vermont and of UVM (1791); his statue stands on the UVM green.

questions.q: During the War of 1812, what happened to Burlington on August 2, 1813?
choices: It burned in a great fire
It was briefly the U.S. capital
The British navy shelled it from the lake
questions.explanation: British ships bombarded Burlington in 1813; the cannons at Battery Park commemorate the American battery that fired back.

questions.q: The northernmost land action of the Civil War happened in Vermont in 1864. What was it?
choices: The St. Albans Raid — Confederates robbed the town's banks
A naval battle on Lake Champlain
A Confederate raid on Montpelier's armory
questions.explanation: In October 1864, Confederate agents from Canada robbed three St. Albans banks of over $200,000 and fled north.

questions.q: Which French explorer gave Lake Champlain its name after reaching it in 1609?
questions.explanation: Samuel de Champlain reached the lake in July 1609 with Algonquin allies and modestly named it for himself.

questions.q: Which Indigenous people are the original inhabitants of the Burlington area and much of Vermont?
questions.explanation: The Western Abenaki called the region home for thousands of years; Vermont formally recognized four Abenaki tribes in 2011–2012.

questions.q: The name 'Winooski' comes from an Abenaki word meaning land of the what?
questions.explanation: Winooski derives from the Abenaki 'winoskik,' meaning 'at the wild onion place' — wild leeks grew along the river.

questions.q: Smugglers' Notch got its name from contraband moved through the pass during which era?
choices: The Embargo of 1807 and War of 1812
questions.explanation: Jefferson's 1807 embargo banned trade with Britain and Canada, so Vermonters smuggled cattle and goods through the notch; Prohibition-era bootleggers later reused the route.

questions.q: In 1870, Burlington was one of the largest ports in America for what commodity?
questions.explanation: Canadian timber floated down the lake made Burlington the third-largest lumber port in the U.S. at its 1870s peak.

questions.q: The Marquis de Lafayette visited Burlington in 1825 and did what at UVM?
choices: Laid the cornerstone of the Old Mill building
questions.explanation: During his 1825 farewell tour of America, Lafayette laid the cornerstone for UVM's Old Mill, which still anchors University Row.

questions.q: Vermont's constitution required its capital to be more central than Burlington. What city became the permanent capital in 1805?
questions.explanation: Montpelier was chosen for its central location in 1805; Windsor had hosted the 1777 constitutional convention.

questions.q: In what Vermont town was the state's 1777 constitution signed, in a tavern now called the 'Birthplace of Vermont'?
questions.explanation: Delegates adopted the constitution at Elijah West's tavern in Windsor in July 1777 — the Old Constitution House still stands there.

questions.q: The Battle of Bennington (1777) is celebrated with a Vermont state holiday — but where was the battle actually fought?
choices: At the base of the Bennington Monument
In New York, about 10 miles from Bennington
questions.explanation: The battle took place in Walloomsac, New York; the stores the British sought were in Bennington, which got the monument and the holiday.

questions.q: What is the name of the 306-foot obelisk that towers over Bennington?
questions.explanation: Dedicated in 1891, the Bennington Battle Monument is the tallest structure in Vermont.

questions.q: Two future U.S. presidents were born in Vermont. Calvin Coolidge is one — who is the other?
questions.explanation: Chester A. Arthur was born in Fairfield, Vermont in 1829; Coolidge in Plymouth Notch in 1872.

questions.q: Where was Calvin Coolidge sworn in as president after Harding's death in 1923?
choices: His father's parlor in Plymouth Notch, by lamplight
Aboard a train in White River Junction
questions.explanation: Coolidge's father, a notary public, administered the oath at 2:47 a.m. on August 3, 1923 in the family homestead.

questions.q: Two founders of major American religious movements were born in Vermont. Joseph Smith (Mormonism) was born in Sharon — who was born in Whitingham?
questions.explanation: Brigham Young, who led the Mormons to Utah, was born in Whitingham, Vermont in 1801.

questions.q: The 'Year Without a Summer,' when snow fell on Vermont in June and crops failed, was which year?
questions.explanation: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora chilled the globe; Vermont saw June 1816 snow and frost every month, driving a wave of westward migration.

questions.q: Which Vermont senator wrote the 1862 act that created America's land-grant colleges?
questions.explanation: Justin Smith Morrill of Strafford authored the Morrill Land-Grant Acts; UVM is Vermont's land-grant university.

questions.q: Vermont's Rokeby Museum in Ferrisburgh preserves a site tied to what 19th-century network?
questions.explanation: The Robinson family farm at Rokeby sheltered fugitives from slavery and is one of the best-documented Underground Railroad sites in the country.

questions.q: In 1823, Alexander Twilight became the first African American to earn a college degree in the U.S. — from which Vermont college?
questions.explanation: Twilight graduated from Middlebury in 1823 and in 1836 became the first Black American elected to a state legislature — Vermont's.

questions.q: Norwich University in Northfield holds what national distinction?
choices: It fielded the first college football team
It admitted the first women cadets in the U.S.
It built the first college observatory
It is the nation's oldest private military college and birthplace of ROTC
questions.explanation: Norwich, founded in 1819, is recognized as the oldest private military college in the United States and the birthplace of ROTC.

questions.q: Burlington's grand Unitarian church at the head of Church Street was completed in what decade?
questions.explanation: The First Unitarian Universalist Society meeting house, finished in 1816, is the oldest house of worship in Burlington and anchors the top of Church Street.

questions.q: What did Burlington's waterfront Moran Plant originally do?
questions.explanation: The Moran Municipal Generating Station burned coal from 1954 to 1986; the hulking shell later became the FRAME overlook.

questions.q: Church Street was closed to cars and opened as a pedestrian marketplace in what year?
questions.explanation: The Church Street Marketplace opened in 1981, converting four blocks into the brick pedestrian mall Burlington is known for.

questions.q: Vermont was the last state in the nation to get which retail giant, in 1995?
questions.explanation: Walmart opened its first Vermont store in Bennington in 1995 — the 50th state it entered, after long local resistance.

questions.q: What Vermont city calls itself the 'Granite Center of the World'?
questions.explanation: Barre's Rock of Ages quarry is one of the largest granite quarries on earth, and Hope Cemetery showcases its carvers' art.

questions.q: Marble from Danby, Vermont covers the exterior of which famous Washington, D.C. building?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court's exterior is Vermont Imperial Danby marble, quarried from the world's largest underground marble quarry.

questions.q: The platform scale, which revolutionized commerce, was invented in 1830 in which Vermont town?
questions.explanation: Thaddeus Fairbanks invented the platform scale in St. Johnsbury; Fairbanks scales built the town, including its Fairbanks Museum.

questions.q: Which Vermont-born blacksmith moved west and built the self-scouring steel plow that 'broke the plains'?
questions.explanation: John Deere was born in Rutland in 1804 and apprenticed in Middlebury before founding his plow works in Illinois.

questions.q: Elisha Otis, born in Halifax, Vermont, made riding in what invention safe?
questions.explanation: Otis's 1852 safety brake stopped elevators from falling if the rope broke, making tall buildings practical.

questions.q: Thomas Davenport of Brandon, Vermont patented an early version of what in 1837?
questions.explanation: Blacksmith Thomas Davenport received the first U.S. patent for an electric motor and used one to run a small electric railway.

questions.q: 'Snowflake' Bentley, the first person to photograph a single snow crystal, lived his whole life in which town near Burlington?
questions.explanation: Wilson 'Snowflake' Bentley photographed over 5,000 snowflakes from his Jericho farm starting in 1885.

questions.q: Philosopher and education reformer John Dewey was born in 1859 in which city?
questions.explanation: Dewey was born in Burlington, graduated from UVM in 1879, and his ashes are interred beside UVM's Ira Allen Chapel.

questions.q: Exiled Soviet author Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn spent 18 years living quietly in which Vermont town?
questions.explanation: Solzhenitsyn wrote in seclusion in Cavendish from 1976 to 1994; townspeople famously refused to give directions to his house.

questions.q: The real Von Trapp family of 'Sound of Music' fame settled in which Vermont town after fleeing Austria?
questions.explanation: The Trapp family bought a Stowe farm in 1942 because it reminded them of Austria; the Trapp Family Lodge still operates there.

questions.q: Who founded the Shelburne Museum, filling 45 acres with Americana — including an entire steamboat?
questions.explanation: Sugar heiress Electra Havemeyer Webb founded the museum in 1947 and had the steamboat Ticonderoga hauled two miles overland to it in 1955.

questions.q: The steamboat parked on the lawn of the Shelburne Museum is named what?
questions.explanation: The Ticonderoga, a 1906 side-paddle-wheel steamer that once worked Lake Champlain, is a National Historic Landmark.

questions.q: Burlington's Fletcher Free Library was built in 1904 with money from which philanthropist's library program?
questions.explanation: The Fletcher Free's grand 1904 building on College Street is a Carnegie library, one of over 1,600 he funded nationwide.

questions.q: Burlington's Flynn, the art deco theater on Main Street, opened in what year?
questions.explanation: The Flynn opened in 1930 as a vaudeville and movie palace and is now the region's flagship performing arts center.

questions.q: In September 2014, Burlington became the first U.S. city of its size to do what?
choices: Source 100% of its electricity from renewables
questions.explanation: When Burlington Electric bought the Winooski One hydro plant in 2014, the city hit 100% renewable electricity — a national first.

questions.q: Burlington's electric utility burns wood chips at which generating station in the Intervale?
questions.explanation: The Joseph C. McNeil Generating Station, opened in 1984, burns woodchips and supplies a large share of Burlington's power.

questions.q: In 2000, Vermont became the first state in the nation to legally recognize what?
questions.explanation: After the Baker v. Vermont ruling, the legislature created civil unions in April 2000 — a national first that roiled state politics.

questions.q: In 2009, Vermont became the first state to legalize same-sex marriage how?
choices: By legislative vote, overriding a veto
questions.explanation: Vermont's legislature overrode Governor Jim Douglas's veto in April 2009 — the first state to enact marriage equality without a court order.

questions.q: What was the 'dome over Winooski' of 1979–80?
choices: A serious proposal to cover the city with a dome to save heating costs
questions.explanation: During the energy crisis, Winooski officials actually studied doming the mile-square city; it won a federal planning grant and international headlines before fizzling.

questions.q: Which state has fewer people than Vermont?
questions.explanation: Vermont (~647,000 people) is the second-least populous state, ahead of only Wyoming.

questions.q: Until 1963, Vermont famously had more of what than people?
questions.explanation: Vermont's dairy herd outnumbered its human population until 1963 — a statistic Vermonters recited with pride.

questions.q: In the 1830s 'Merino craze,' Vermont's hills carried roughly how many sheep?
choices: Over a million — about six per person
questions.explanation: The wool boom peaked around 1840 with 1.7 million sheep; its collapse helped depopulate hill farms.

questions.q: Vermont's forests tell a comeback story. The state went from about 80% cleared in the 1800s to about how much forested today?
questions.explanation: After sheep farming collapsed, forests reclaimed the hills — Vermont flipped from ~20% wooded to roughly three-quarters wooded.

questions.q: Ben & Jerry's thanks its customers every spring with what giveaway, started in 1979?
questions.explanation: Free Cone Day marked the shop's first anniversary in 1979 and became a worldwide tradition.

questions.q: Which interstate runs past Burlington, connecting it to Montpelier and, eventually, Boston?
questions.explanation: I-89 links Burlington to Montpelier and White River Junction; I-91 runs up Vermont's eastern edge.

questions.q: Three interstates touch Vermont. I-89, I-91, and which surprise third, for a few miles near St. Johnsbury?
questions.explanation: I-93's final 11 miles cross into Vermont to meet I-91 near St. Johnsbury.

questions.q: Lake Champlain contains roughly how many islands?
questions.explanation: The lake holds some 70-plus islands, from Grand Isle down to bare rock ledges like the Four Brothers.

questions.q: Burlington draws its drinking water from where?
questions.explanation: The city treats lake water; keeping Champlain clean is quite literally a matter of taste.

questions.q: The biggest ongoing threat to Lake Champlain's summer swimming is what?
choices: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) blooms fed by phosphorus runoff
questions.explanation: Phosphorus from farms and pavement feeds blue-green algae blooms that periodically close beaches, especially on shallow bays.

questions.q: Which invasive creature, arriving via the Champlain Canal, coats Lake Champlain rocks and cuts swimmers' feet?
questions.explanation: Zebra mussels reached the lake in 1993 and carpeted its hard surfaces within years.

questions.q: The parasitic fish that Lake Champlain managers spend millions controlling to protect salmon and trout is the…
questions.explanation: Sea lamprey latch onto salmonids and leave telltale wounds; control programs treat tributaries on a rotating basis.

questions.q: Burlington's breakwater, protecting the harbor since the 1800s, is guarded at each end by what?
questions.explanation: The north and south breakwater lights (rebuilt in 2003 to historic designs) still mark Burlington Harbor.

questions.q: What runs along Burlington's entire lakefront, from Oakledge to the Winooski River mouth?
questions.explanation: The 8-mile Burlington Greenway bike path strings together the city's waterfront parks along the old rail bed.

questions.q: Vermont's 'Crown Jewel' state-owned scenic drive climbs to a chin-height parking lot on which mountain via a toll road?
questions.explanation: The Mount Mansfield Auto Toll Road, run by Stowe, has carried visitors toward the summit ridge since the carriage era. Camel's Hump, by contrast, has no development at all.

questions.q: Vermont's most-photographed fall scene may be Sleepy Hollow Farm, a dirt-road postcard near which tourist town?
questions.explanation: The Pomfret farm near Woodstock got so mobbed by influencers that the road is now closed to visitors each foliage season.

questions.q: What do Vermonters call visitors who clog the roads each October?
questions.explanation: Leaf peepers pump roughly half a billion dollars into Vermont's economy every fall — honk gently.

questions.q: Stowe's most famous run collection, the 'Front Four,' consists of Starr, Goat, National, and…
questions.explanation: The Front Four — Starr, Goat, National, Liftline — are Mansfield's classic double-black test pieces.

questions.q: The Von Trapp family's Stowe lodge added what distinctly Austrian-Vermont business in 2010?
questions.explanation: Von Trapp Brewing makes Austrian-style lagers — 'a little of Austria, a lot of Vermont.'

questions.q: Vermont's celebrated 'town meeting' government descends most directly from what?
questions.explanation: Vermont towns imported the New England town meeting wholesale; many still vote budgets from the floor.

questions.q: What percentage of Vermont's electricity came from Vermont Yankee before the nuclear plant closed in 2014?
questions.explanation: Vermont Yankee in Vernon produced more than 70% of the electricity generated in Vermont; its closure reshaped the state's energy debate.

questions.q: Burlington's sister city of Yaroslavl is located in which country?
questions.explanation: The 1988 Burlington–Yaroslavl pairing was a late-Cold-War citizen-diplomacy gesture; the relationship was suspended after 2022.

questions.q: Lake Champlain's water eventually reaches which ocean?
choices: The Atlantic, via the St. Lawrence
questions.explanation: North through the Richelieu to the St. Lawrence and out past Quebec — Champlain drains toward the North Atlantic.

questions.q: The Champlain Canal, opened in 1823, connects the lake's south end to what?
questions.explanation: The canal links Whitehall to the Hudson at Fort Edward, which once made Burlington a booming inland port.

questions.q: What is Vermont's largest county by population, home to a quarter of the state?
questions.explanation: Chittenden County — Burlington and its suburbs — holds about 170,000 people.

questions.q: Vermont's smallest county by population, with fewer than 6,000 people, is which NEK outpost?
questions.explanation: Essex County in the far Northeast Kingdom is Vermont's emptiest — fewer residents than a UVM class year.

questions.q: The gulf that separates 'town' and 'gown' Burlington is bridged every fall when UVM students moving in cause what phenomenon?
choices: Couch-lined curbs and the citywide 'move-in' furniture swap
questions.explanation: Late-August Burlington is famous for curbside couch archaeology as 5,000 students shuffle apartments.

questions.q: What institution is Vermont's largest private employer?
choices: The University of Vermont Medical Center / UVM Health Network
questions.explanation: The UVM Health Network, anchored by the Burlington hospital, employs more Vermonters than any other private organization.

questions.q: Route 100, beloved by foliage drivers, runs where?
choices: North–south up the spine of the Green Mountains
questions.explanation: Route 100 threads the mountain valleys past Stowe, Waterbury, and the Mad River Valley — Vermont's classic scenic drive.

questions.q: The Ben & Jerry's factory tour, one of Vermont's top tourist attractions, is in which town on Route 100?
questions.explanation: The Waterbury factory has offered tours since 1986, complete with the Flavor Graveyard out back.

questions.q: Vermont's legislature meets in a State House fronted by a statue of which Revolutionary hero?
questions.explanation: A marble Ethan Allen guards the State House portico (the current statue is a 1941 replacement of an 1861 original).

questions.q: What happened to Ethan Allen after the Revolution?
choices: He farmed in Burlington and died there in 1789
questions.explanation: Allen retired to his Intervale farm and died in February 1789; he's buried under a monument in Burlington's Greenmount Cemetery.

questions.q: Ethan Allen is buried in which Burlington cemetery, beneath a 42-foot column?
questions.explanation: The Ethan Allen Monument in Greenmount Cemetery on Colchester Avenue marks (approximately) his grave — no one is certain exactly where he lies.

questions.q: Vermont's most expensive public works disaster-recovery in state history followed which event?
choices: The 1927 flood (in nominal dollars it was Irene)
questions.explanation: Irene damaged or destroyed more than 500 miles of highway and 200 bridges; rebuilding cost hundreds of millions.

questions.q: The 'Great Vermont Flood' of July 2023 drew constant comparison to which benchmark disaster?
questions.explanation: Montpelier's 2023 inundation was widely measured against November 1927, still Vermont's deadliest flood.

questions.q: Which Burlington venue hosted UVM basketball and big concerts downtown from 1927 until its 2016 closure over structural concerns?
questions.explanation: Memorial Auditorium at Main and South Union hosted everything from Nirvana to wrestling before closing in 2016; its future is a perennial city debate.

questions.q: Burlington incorporated as a city (separating from the town that became South Burlington) in what year?
questions.explanation: Burlington took a city charter in 1865; the remaining rural town eventually became South Burlington.

questions.q: The Old Round Church, a 16-sided 1813 landmark often called America's first community church in the round, stands in which town?
questions.explanation: Richmond's Old Round Church was built by five denominations together; legend says the shape left no corner for the devil.

questions.q: Vermont's official state pie and state fruit are, fittingly…
questions.explanation: The apple does double duty: state fruit (1999) and the filling of the state pie.

questions.q: The traditional Vermont dish 'salt pork and milk gravy' belongs to which meal tradition, still served at church suppers?
choices: Boiled dinner and sugar-on-snow suppers of old Vermont farm cooking
questions.explanation: Old Vermont farmhouse cooking — boiled dinners, salt pork, johnnycakes — survives at town church suppers, alongside French-Canadian tourtière in many families.

questions.q: What is the highest peak in Vermont?
questions.explanation: Mount Mansfield tops out at 4,393 feet; its summit ridge resembles a face, with the Chin as the highest point.

questions.q: Mount Mansfield's summit ridge is said to look like a human face. Which 'feature' is the actual highest point?
questions.explanation: The Chin (4,393 ft) is Vermont's highest point; the Nose hosts the broadcast towers.

questions.q: How deep is Lake Champlain at its deepest point?
questions.explanation: The lake reaches roughly 400 feet deep between Charlotte, VT and Essex, NY — deep enough to stay mysterious.

questions.q: About how long is Lake Champlain from end to end?
questions.explanation: The lake runs about 120 miles from Whitehall, NY north into Quebec's Missisquoi Bay.

questions.q: For 18 days in 1998, Lake Champlain officially held what title?
choices: The deepest lake in New England
questions.explanation: President Clinton signed a bill declaring Champlain a Great Lake in March 1998 (for research funding); Congress rescinded it 18 days later after Midwest outrage.

questions.q: Lake Champlain drains north into the St. Lawrence River via which river?
questions.explanation: The lake's outlet is the Richelieu River, flowing north through Quebec to the St. Lawrence.

questions.q: Isle La Motte in Lake Champlain is home to the Chazy Reef, notable as what?
choices: One of the oldest known coral reefs on Earth
questions.explanation: The Chazy Fossil Reef formed about 480 million years ago in a tropical sea and is among the oldest reefs where corals appeared.

questions.q: What is the name of Lake Champlain's legendary monster?
questions.explanation: 'Champ' has been 'sighted' for two centuries; both Vermont and New York have passed resolutions protecting it.

questions.q: The famous 1977 photograph claimed to show Champ was taken by whom?
questions.explanation: Sandra Mansi's photo, taken near St. Albans, remains the most famous piece of Champ 'evidence' and ran in the New York Times.

questions.q: Which river empties into Lake Champlain between Burlington and Colchester?
questions.explanation: The Winooski River, 90 miles long, cuts through the Green Mountains and reaches the lake just north of Burlington.

questions.q: What is the longest river that flows entirely within Vermont?
questions.explanation: Otter Creek runs about 112 miles from Mount Tabor north to Lake Champlain at Ferrisburgh.

questions.q: The Connecticut River forms Vermont's eastern border — but which state actually owns the river?
choices: They split it down the middle
questions.explanation: A 1934 Supreme Court ruling set the boundary at the Vermont shore's low-water mark, so the river itself belongs to New Hampshire.

questions.q: Vermont is the only New England state without what?
questions.explanation: Vermont is landlocked — the only one of the six New England states with no ocean shoreline.

questions.q: How many towns does the fabled '251 Club' challenge Vermonters to visit?
questions.explanation: The 251 Club, founded in 1954, celebrates visiting all 251 of Vermont's towns and cities (the count including cities and towns).

questions.q: How many counties does Vermont have?
questions.explanation: Vermont's 14 counties range from populous Chittenden to tiny Essex in the Northeast Kingdom.

questions.q: Who coined the nickname 'Northeast Kingdom' for Vermont's three northeastern counties?
questions.explanation: George Aiken used the phrase in a 1949 speech; it stuck for Essex, Orleans, and Caledonia counties.

questions.q: Which three counties make up the Northeast Kingdom?
questions.explanation: The Kingdom is Essex, Orleans, and Caledonia counties — Vermont's wildest corner.

questions.q: What is Vermont's second-largest city by population?
questions.explanation: South Burlington (about 20,000 people) passed Rutland after the 2020 census to become Vermont's number two city.

questions.q: Montpelier holds what distinction among U.S. state capitals?
questions.explanation: With about 8,000 residents, Montpelier is the least populous state capital in America.

questions.q: Montpelier is famously the only state capital without what?
questions.explanation: Montpelier remains the only U.S. state capital with no McDonald's — a point of some local pride.

questions.q: Which Vermont municipality, chartered in 1788, is one of the smallest cities in the entire U.S.?
questions.explanation: Vergennes covers about 2.5 square miles with roughly 2,500 people, and claims to be Vermont's oldest city.

questions.q: In 2022, which village became Vermont's newest (10th) city?
questions.explanation: Essex Junction separated from the Town of Essex and incorporated as a city on July 1, 2022.

questions.q: Quechee Gorge, 'Vermont's Little Grand Canyon,' is about how deep?
questions.explanation: The Ottauquechee River carved the 165-foot gorge; the Route 4 bridge over it is a favorite viewpoint.

questions.q: What is the deepest lake located entirely within Vermont?
questions.explanation: Fjord-like Lake Willoughby in Westmore plunges over 300 feet deep between Mounts Pisgah and Hor.

questions.q: Lake Memphremagog, shared with Canada, has its Vermont shore at which city?
questions.explanation: Newport sits at the south end of Memphremagog; most of the 31-mile lake lies in Quebec.

questions.q: In Derby Line, Vermont, the Haskell Free Library and Opera House is famous because…
choices: The U.S.–Canada border runs right through the building
It's the smallest library in America
questions.explanation: A black line across the reading room marks the international border; the stage is in Canada while most seats are in the U.S.

questions.q: The Long Trail, running the length of Vermont, holds what national distinction?
choices: Oldest long-distance hiking trail in the U.S.
questions.explanation: The Green Mountain Club built the 272-mile Long Trail between 1910 and 1930, inspiring the Appalachian Trail.

questions.q: For about 100 miles in southern Vermont, the Long Trail shares its route with which famous footpath?
questions.explanation: The AT and Long Trail coincide from the Massachusetts line to Maine Junction near Killington, where the AT turns east.

questions.q: Which distinctively double-humped mountain appears on Vermont's state quarter?
questions.explanation: The 2001 Vermont quarter shows maple sugaring with Camel's Hump — one of the state's few undeveloped high summits — in the background.

questions.q: Early French explorers had their own name for Camel's Hump. What did they call it?
choices: 'Le dos de baleine' — the whale's back
questions.explanation: French explorers dubbed the double summit 'le lion couchant,' the crouching (or sleeping) lion; 'Camel's Rump' came later, politely softened to Camel's Hump.

questions.q: Burlington sits on a hillside facing which mountain range across Lake Champlain?
questions.explanation: Burlington's famous sunsets drop behind New York's Adirondacks; the Greens rise behind the city to the east.

questions.q: What was Burlington's population in the 2020 census?
questions.explanation: Burlington counted 44,743 residents in 2020 — the least populous 'largest city of a state' in America.

questions.q: Burlington is the least populous city in America to hold what title?
choices: Host of an NCAA Division I school
questions.explanation: No other state's biggest city is as small as Burlington (~44,700 people).

questions.q: Vermont's tallest building, the 11-story Decker Towers in Burlington, holds what national distinction?
choices: Tallest wooden building in the U.S.
questions.explanation: At about 124 feet, Decker Towers is the shortest building to rank as any state's tallest.

questions.q: Burlington International Airport (BTV) is actually located in which municipality?
questions.explanation: The airport sits entirely in South Burlington, though Burlington owns and operates it — a long-running local quirk.

questions.q: The Island Line Trail heads out of Burlington across the lake on what unusual surface?
questions.explanation: The old Rutland Railroad's Colchester causeway — built from marble riprap — carries the bike path 3 miles into the lake, with a seasonal bike ferry crossing 'the Cut' to South Hero.

questions.q: Which four Lake Champlain islands/towns make up Grand Isle County?
choices: South Hero, Grand Isle, North Hero, Isle La Motte (plus Alburgh)
questions.explanation: Grand Isle County comprises the island towns of South Hero, Grand Isle, North Hero, and Isle La Motte, plus the Alburgh peninsula.

questions.q: North Hero and South Hero are said to be named for which 'heroes'?
choices: Green Mountain Boys killed at Bennington
questions.explanation: The islands' 1779 grant honored Revolutionary heroes — traditionally the Allen brothers, both grantees.

questions.q: The Champlain Thrust fault, where 500-million-year-old rock sits atop younger rock, is famously visible at which Burlington-area spot?
questions.explanation: At Lone Rock Point, older dolostone rides over younger shale — one of the world's most accessible thrust-fault exposures, on Episcopal diocese land.

questions.q: Mount Philo in Charlotte became Vermont's first what, in 1924?
questions.explanation: Mount Philo State Park, with its sweeping Champlain Valley views, was Vermont's first state park.

questions.q: Vermont shares an international border with which Canadian province?
questions.explanation: Vermont's 90-mile northern border is entirely with Quebec.

questions.q: The name 'Vermont' most likely comes from French words meaning what?
questions.explanation: 'Verd mont' — green mountain. Dr. Thomas Young proposed 'Vermont' in 1777.

questions.q: What is Burlington's longstanding nickname?
questions.explanation: Burlington has been called the Queen City since the 19th century, a nickname for grand lake-side cities.

questions.q: Which Burlington park sits on a bluff where cannons once defended the city, overlooking the lake at the north end of Battery Street?
questions.explanation: Battery Park is named for the American artillery battery that fired on British ships there in 1813.

questions.q: The stone lookout tower in Burlington's New North End, built in 1905 on land once owned by a famous Vermonter, is called what?
questions.explanation: Ethan Allen Tower in Ethan Allen Park stands on the Allen farm's former land, with views over the Winooski valley.

questions.q: Lake Champlain forms most of the border between Vermont and which state?
questions.explanation: Roughly half of Vermont's western border with New York runs through Lake Champlain.

questions.q: Ben & Jerry's opened its first scoop shop in 1978 in what kind of renovated Burlington building?
questions.explanation: Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield opened in a renovated gas station at St. Paul and College Streets on May 5, 1978.

questions.q: Ben and Jerry learned to make ice cream from a $5 correspondence course offered by which university?
questions.explanation: The pair split a $5 Penn State correspondence course on ice cream making before opening their Burlington shop.

questions.q: Cherry Garcia, honoring Jerry Garcia, was reportedly the first ice cream flavor named after what?
questions.explanation: Introduced in 1987 after fans suggested it on a scoop-shop bulletin board, Cherry Garcia was the first flavor named for a rock musician.

questions.q: What does Ben & Jerry's keep behind its Waterbury factory?
choices: A Flavor Graveyard for retired flavors
questions.explanation: Discontinued flavors get granite headstones in the Flavor Graveyard — RIP Wavy Gravy.

questions.q: The 'Vermonster,' Ben & Jerry's legendary sundae bucket, contains how many scoops?
questions.explanation: The Vermonster packs 20 scoops plus a full complement of toppings into one bucket.

questions.q: Which multinational bought Ben & Jerry's in 2000?
questions.explanation: Unilever acquired Ben & Jerry's in 2000, with an independent board preserving the social mission.

questions.q: What is a 'creemee'?
choices: Vermont's name for soft-serve ice cream
questions.explanation: In Vermont soft-serve is a creemee — and the maple creemee is the state's unofficial summer dessert.

questions.q: Vermont produces roughly what share of the United States' maple syrup?
questions.explanation: Vermont is the runaway #1 producer, typically making around 50% of U.S. maple syrup — over 3 million gallons in recent years.

questions.q: About how many gallons of sap does it take to make one gallon of maple syrup?
questions.explanation: The classic ratio is roughly 40 to 1, since sap is only about 2% sugar.

questions.q: Under the maple grading system Vermont adopted in 2014, what happened to old 'Grade B' syrup?
choices: It became 'Grade A Very Dark, Strong Taste'
It's now sold only to bakeries
It was banned from retail sale
questions.explanation: The new system makes everything Grade A with descriptive color/taste names; the old Grade B became 'Very Dark, Strong Taste.' 'Fancy' was the old lightest grade.

questions.q: What is 'sugar on snow'?
choices: Hot syrup poured on snow to make taffy, served with pickles and doughnuts
questions.explanation: At sugarhouse parties, boiled syrup is drizzled on packed snow to form chewy taffy — traditionally cut with a dill pickle.

questions.q: Vermont law says restaurants making a 'good faith effort' should serve apple pie with which of these?
choices: Cold milk, cheddar cheese, or vanilla ice cream
questions.explanation: A 1999 state law (Act 15) declares apple pie the state pie and lists milk, at least half an ounce of cheddar, or ice cream as proper accompaniments.

questions.q: Cabot Creamery, famous for its cheddar, is what kind of business?
questions.explanation: Cabot has been a farmer-owned co-op since 1919, now part of Agri-Mark with over 500 member farms.

questions.q: Which Greensboro, Vermont brewery's 'Hill Farmstead' beers have repeatedly been ranked best in the world?
questions.explanation: Shaun Hill's Hill Farmstead in Greensboro has been named the world's best brewery multiple times by RateBeer.

questions.q: Heady Topper, the double IPA that launched a thousand beer pilgrimages, is brewed by which Vermont brewery?
questions.explanation: The Alchemist in Stowe (originally Waterbury) brews Heady Topper, long ranked among the world's best beers.

questions.q: What instruction is printed on every can of Heady Topper?
questions.explanation: John Kimmich insists the hop aroma keeps best when you drink straight from the silver can.

questions.q: Vermont's first brewpub, opened in Burlington in 1988 by brewing pioneer Greg Noonan, is called what?
questions.explanation: Greg Noonan's Vermont Pub & Brewery on College Street opened in 1988 after he helped change state law to allow brewpubs.

questions.q: Magic Hat Brewing, long of South Burlington, was best known for which cryptically named flagship beer?
questions.explanation: Magic Hat #9, a 'not quite pale ale' with apricot notes, was the brewery's flagship from the 1990s.

questions.q: Lawson's Finest Liquids, maker of Sip of Sunshine, has its taproom in which Mad River Valley town?
questions.explanation: Lawson's opened its Waitsfield brewery and taproom in 2018; Sip of Sunshine is its cult IPA.

questions.q: Which cidery poured its first pints in Burlington in 2011 and is known for 'Unified Press'?
questions.explanation: Citizen Cider grew from a Pine Street operation into one of the Northeast's biggest independent cideries; Unified Press is the flagship.

questions.q: Woodchuck, one of America's best-selling hard ciders, is made in which Vermont town?
questions.explanation: Woodchuck Hard Cider has been made in Middlebury since 1991 and helped kick off the U.S. cider revival.

questions.q: Al's French Frys, the South Burlington institution slinging fries since the 1940s, spells 'Frys' that way because…
choices: A sign painter ran out of room
That's how the founders spelled it, and it stuck
questions.explanation: Al and Genevieve Rusterholz's quirky spelling became the brand; the James Beard Foundation named Al's an 'American Classic' in 2010.

questions.q: Beansie's Bus, a Burlington summer fixture since 1944, sells food from what?
choices: A cart at City Hall Park
A converted school bus at Battery Park
questions.explanation: The green Beansie's school bus has parked at Battery Park each summer for generations, serving fries, dogs, and burgers.

questions.q: Nectar's, the Main Street club where Phish got its start, is equally famous for serving what?
questions.explanation: Fries smothered in gravy have been the Nectar's late-night order since Nectar Rorris ran the grill.

questions.q: Which downtown Burlington restaurant, a Church Street corner fixture since 1980, styles itself a 'bistro and café' with a Parisian feel?
questions.explanation: Leunig's Bistro has anchored the corner of Church and College since 1980, cherished for its bohemian Paris-café vibe.

questions.q: American Flatbread, whose Burlington hearth draws nightly crowds, bakes its pizzas how?
questions.explanation: George Schenk founded American Flatbread in Waitsfield baking on a primitive wood-fired hearth; the Burlington outpost keeps the flame.

questions.q: The Skinny Pancake, now all over Vermont, started in 2003 as what?
choices: A crepe cart on Church Street
questions.explanation: Brothers Benjy and Jonny Adler started with a pushcart crepe stand on Church Street before opening the waterfront restaurant.

questions.q: Burlington's downtown grocery co-op, owned by its members since 1973, is called what?
questions.explanation: Onion River Co-op began in 1973 and now runs the two City Market stores — one of the largest single-store co-ops in the country.

questions.q: Lake Champlain Chocolates, the Burlington chocolatier founded in 1983, has its factory and flagship store on which street?
questions.explanation: The Pine Street factory store anchors Burlington's South End 'arts and eats' corridor.

questions.q: What cheese fact makes Cabot's 'Seriously Sharp' and other Vermont cheddars white rather than orange?
choices: Vermont cheddar traditionally skips annatto dye
questions.explanation: Orange cheddar is just dyed with annatto; New England tradition leaves cheddar its natural white.

questions.q: Shelburne Farms, the 1,400-acre nonprofit farm south of Burlington, was originally built as what?
choices: A Gilded Age Vanderbilt-family model farm
questions.explanation: Dr. William Seward Webb and Lila Vanderbilt Webb built the estate in 1886 as a model agricultural farm; it's now an education nonprofit famous for cheddar.

questions.q: The gleaming diner that has served Bank Street since 1925 is called what?
questions.explanation: Henry's Diner has been a downtown Burlington fixture since 1925, one of Vermont's classic barrel-roof diners.

questions.q: King Arthur Baking Company, America's oldest flour company, is headquartered in which Vermont town?
questions.explanation: Founded in Boston in 1790, the 100% employee-owned company moved to Norwich, Vermont, where its campus and baking school draw pilgrims.

questions.q: Vermont Common Crackers, the little round crackers once sold from cracker barrels, are a specialty of which store?
questions.explanation: The Vermont Country Store in Weston revived the 1828-style common cracker, complete with the original machinery.

questions.q: Cold Hollow Cider Mill in Waterbury Center is a mecca for which snack?
questions.explanation: Cold Hollow presses cider year-round and its cider doughnuts are a Route 100 rite of passage.

questions.q: Vermont's iconic snack-bar order 'a maple creemee with maple sprinkles' uses sprinkles made from what?
questions.explanation: The good stands crumble real maple sugar over the creemee — accept no waxy substitute.

questions.q: Which company, founded in Waterbury in 1981, became a coffee giant before merging into Keurig Dr Pepper?
questions.explanation: Green Mountain Coffee Roasters started in a Waterbury café, later acquired Keurig, and became Keurig Green Mountain.

questions.q: The gently anarchic bumper sticker slogan seen on Vermont creemee stands, 'Eat More…' what?
questions.explanation: The 'Eat More Kale' shirts of Montpelier artist Bo Muller-Moore became a Vermont icon — especially after Chick-fil-A picked a trademark fight over 'Eat Mor Chikin' and lost the PR war.

questions.q: What did Burlington's storied hot-dog-cart proprietor Lois Bodoky, immortalized on a Church Street plaque, sell for decades?
questions.explanation: 'Lois the hot dog lady' served Church Street from her cart for over 30 years; after her death in 2016 the city honored her with a memorial marker.

questions.q: Bove's, the beloved red-sauce restaurant that fed Burlington from 1941 to 2015, lives on today how?
choices: Its pasta sauces are sold in stores
questions.explanation: The Bove family closed the Pearl Street restaurant in 2015 but still jars its marinara and vodka sauces.

questions.q: Vermont's official state beverage is what?
questions.explanation: The legislature named milk the state beverage in 1983 — dairy remains Vermont's biggest agricultural sector.

questions.q: What is 'switchel'?
choices: A haymaker's drink of water, vinegar, ginger, and maple
questions.explanation: Switchel (or 'haymaker's punch') refreshed Vermont field crews for generations and has enjoyed a hipster revival.

questions.q: The UVM Dairy Bar tradition lives on in which campus creemee flavor pairing known as a 'maple twist'?
questions.explanation: A maple-vanilla twist is the standard order at Vermont creemee windows, UVM's included.

questions.q: Which Winooski restaurant block earned that city a reputation as Chittenden County's food destination in the 2010s?
questions.explanation: Restaurants ringing Winooski's roundabout — Misery Loves Co., Waterworks, and others — made the little city a dining destination.

questions.q: Vermont was the first state to require labeling of what, with a 2014 law that took effect in 2016?
questions.explanation: Vermont's Act 120 was the nation's first GMO labeling mandate; it pushed Congress to pass a national standard.

questions.q: UVM's initials don't stand for 'University of Vermont.' What Latin phrase do they abbreviate?
questions.explanation: UVM stands for Universitas Viridis Montis — 'University of the Green Mountains.'

questions.q: UVM was chartered in what year, the same year Vermont joined the Union?
questions.explanation: Ira Allen founded UVM in 1791, making it the fifth-oldest university in New England.

questions.q: What is UVM's athletic mascot?
questions.explanation: UVM teams are the Catamounts — the old New England name for the mountain lion. Rally is the costumed cat.

questions.q: UVM's Billings Library, a Romanesque masterpiece on University Row, was designed by which famed American architect?
questions.explanation: Henry Hobson Richardson designed Billings (1885), one of the finest examples of Richardsonian Romanesque on any campus.

questions.q: Which famous American philosopher, UVM Class of 1879, has his ashes interred beside Ira Allen Chapel on campus?
questions.explanation: Burlington-born John Dewey is the rare major philosopher buried on the campus of his alma mater.

questions.q: In 1875, UVM was the first university in the country to admit women to what?
questions.explanation: UVM's Phi Beta Kappa chapter was the first to elect women, four years after the university began admitting women students in 1871.

questions.q: UVM's beloved winter tradition sees students pour onto the main green whenever what happens?
choices: The first real snowfall sparks a campus-wide snowball fight
questions.explanation: The first snow of the year traditionally triggers a mass snowball fight on the UVM green.

questions.q: UVM's hockey barn, opened in 1963 and one of college hockey's loudest, is nicknamed what?
questions.explanation: Gutterson Fieldhouse — 'the Gut' — is home ice for Catamount hockey.

questions.q: Which private Burlington college in the Hill Section is known for game design and cybersecurity programs?
questions.explanation: Champlain College, founded 1878, occupies Victorian mansions in Burlington's Hill Section.

questions.q: Saint Michael's College, the Catholic college founded in 1904 by the Society of Saint Edmund, is located in which town?
questions.explanation: St. Mike's campus sits in Colchester, near Fort Ethan Allen.

questions.q: Phish formed in 1983 at UVM. Where did they play their first gig that December?
questions.explanation: On December 2, 1983 the band played a dorm semi-formal at the Harris-Millis cafeteria — using a hockey stick as a mic stand.

questions.q: Which four musicians make up Phish's classic lineup?
choices: Trey Anastasio, Mike Gordon, Jon Fishman, Jeff Holdsworth
Trey Anastasio, Mike Gordon, Jeff Holdsworth, Marc Daubert
Trey Anastasio, Mike Gordon, Jon Fishman, Page McConnell
Trey Anastasio, Les Claypool, Stewart Copeland, Page McConnell
questions.explanation: Keyboardist Page McConnell completed the quartet in 1985; founding guitarist Jeff Holdsworth left in 1986.

questions.q: Phish's 1992 album 'A Picture of Nectar' is named in honor of whom?
choices: Nectar Rorris, owner of the Burlington bar where they cut their teeth
questions.explanation: The album thanks Nectar Rorris of Nectar's, who gave Phish its formative residency; his face hides in the orange on the cover.

questions.q: Phish drummer Jon Fishman performs in what signature garment?
choices: A dress patterned with red donuts
questions.explanation: Fishman's donut-patterned muumuu is so iconic the 'Fishman donut' became the band's unofficial logo; he also plays vacuum cleaner solos.

questions.q: The mythical land in Trey Anastasio's Phish song cycle, populated by the Lizards, is called what?
questions.explanation: Gamehendge, from Anastasio's senior thesis 'The Man Who Stepped Into Yesterday,' is Phish's mythology; Icculus is its prophet.

questions.q: Phish's 2004 'farewell' festival (before their 2009 return) was held in which Northeast Kingdom town?
questions.explanation: The mud-soaked Coventry festival drew 65,000+ fans; when parking fields flooded, thousands abandoned cars on I-91 and hiked in.

questions.q: Ben & Jerry's honored Phish with which flavor in 1997?
questions.explanation: Phish Food — chocolate ice cream with marshmallow, caramel, and fudge fish — sends its royalties toward Lake Champlain cleanup via the WaterWheel Foundation.

questions.q: Grace Potter, the rock singer from Waitsfield, co-founded which Burlington waterfront festival in 2011?
questions.explanation: Grand Point North brings Potter home to Waterfront Park each September.

questions.q: Which Burlington-born hip-hop collective signed with Warner Records in 2019 after breaking out with 'Champion'?
questions.explanation: 99 Neighbors formed around Burlington and South Burlington friends and rose from SoundCloud to Warner.

questions.q: The jam band Twiddle, beloved by the Phish-adjacent crowd, formed at which Vermont college?
questions.explanation: Twiddle formed at Castleton in 2004 and became a Vermont jam institution.

questions.q: Burlington's premier concert club, which moved from Winooski to South Burlington in 2004, is called what?
questions.explanation: Higher Ground has anchored the local live-music scene since 1998, hosting everyone from Wilco to Snoop Dogg.

questions.q: The Burlington Discover Jazz Festival has filled downtown with music each June since what decade?
questions.explanation: Discover Jazz launched in 1984 and has brought legends like Dizzy Gillespie and Wynton Marsalis to the Flynn and Church Street.

questions.q: 'Moonlight in Vermont,' the 1944 standard recorded by Sinatra and Ella, is unusual among popular songs because…
questions.explanation: The lyric is entirely unrhymed, and its verses are haiku-like six-syllable images of the state.

questions.q: Which Vermont songwriter's folk opera grew into the Tony Award-winning Broadway musical 'Hadestown'?
questions.explanation: Anaïs Mitchell of Addison County staged early versions of Hadestown in Vermont barns and town halls in 2006–07 before Broadway; it won 8 Tonys in 2019.

questions.q: Bread and Puppet Theater, famous for giant papier-mâché puppets and radical pageants, is based in which Northeast Kingdom town?
questions.explanation: Peter Schumann's Bread and Puppet has performed from its Glover farm since 1974, serving free sourdough with every show.

questions.q: Vermont's official state song, adopted in 2000 after a statewide contest, is called what?
questions.explanation: Diane Martin's 'These Green Mountains' won the contest and replaced 'Hail, Vermont!' as the official state song.

questions.q: Burlington City Arts runs its downtown gallery out of which repurposed 1889 building?
choices: The old Ethan Allen firehouse on Church Street
questions.explanation: The BCA Center occupies the former Ethan Allen Engine Company No. 4 firehouse at 135 Church Street.

questions.q: Which September event turns Burlington's Pine Street corridor into a giant open studio?
questions.explanation: SEABA's Art Hop has showcased South End studios, galleries, and warehouses every September since 1993.

questions.q: Waking Windows, the indie music festival that takes over an entire downtown each spring, happens where?
questions.explanation: Waking Windows sprawls across Winooski's bars, restaurants, and rooftops each May.

questions.q: The Festival of Fools brings what to Church Street every August?
choices: Street performers — jugglers, acrobats, and comedy busking
questions.explanation: Modeled on international busker fests, the Festival of Fools has filled the Marketplace with circus arts since 2007.

questions.q: UVM's Fleming Museum has long fascinated Burlington schoolkids with which resident artifact?
questions.explanation: The Fleming's Egyptian mummy has been a fixture of school field trips for generations.

questions.q: UVM's Larner College of Medicine, founded in 1822, ranks where among America's oldest medical schools?
questions.explanation: Founded in 1822, UVM's medical college is the seventh-oldest in the United States.

questions.q: What happened to UVM football?
choices: It plays in the Ivy League
questions.explanation: UVM dropped football in 1974 for budget reasons — one reason hockey, basketball, and soccer loom so large in Burlington.

questions.q: UVM's 'Kake Walk,' abolished in 1969, is remembered as what?
choices: A blackface minstrel tradition the university renounced
questions.explanation: Kake Walk, once the centerpiece of Winter Carnival, involved blackface performance; UVM ended it in 1969 and has formally apologized.

questions.q: The gold-domed building crowning UVM's University Row, whose cornerstone Lafayette laid in 1825, is called what?
questions.explanation: Old Mill's lantern dome is visible across Burlington; it houses the College of Arts and Sciences.

questions.q: Which member of Phish bought his town's general store in 2022 and has served on its selectboard?
questions.explanation: Drummer Jon Fishman and his wife bought the Lincoln General Store to keep the town's gathering place alive.

questions.q: Vermont's independent rock station 'The Point,' broadcasting since 1979, uses which call letters?
questions.explanation: WNCS 104.7 'The Point' has championed independent music in Vermont since 1979; WIZN is the classic-rock 'Wizard.'

questions.q: UVM's student radio station, on air since 1955 with a strict no-mainstream ethos, is called what?
questions.explanation: WRUV 90.1 FM, 'Burlington's Basement,' is UVM's freeform student station.

questions.q: The 'Battle for the Cup' between UVM and Saint Michael's is contested in which sport?
questions.explanation: The cross-town basketball rivalry, revived in recent decades as an exhibition, is Chittenden County's version of a derby.

questions.q: Trey Anastasio came to Burlington as a transfer student and finished his degree where, studying composition with Ernie Stires?
questions.explanation: Anastasio (and Fishman) finished at Goddard College in Plainfield; his senior study there produced the Gamehendge saga.

questions.q: Nectar's, launchpad of Phish, sits on which Burlington street beneath its famous rotating neon sign?
questions.explanation: Nectar's and its landmark sign have anchored lower Main Street since 1975.

questions.q: Bernie Sanders was elected mayor of Burlington in 1981 by how many votes?
questions.explanation: Sanders beat five-term Democratic incumbent Gordon Paquette by just 10 votes in March 1981.

questions.q: How many terms did Bernie Sanders serve as Burlington's mayor?
questions.explanation: Sanders won four two-year terms, serving from 1981 to 1989.

questions.q: In 1987, Mayor Bernie Sanders recorded a folk album. What was it called?
questions.explanation: 'We Shall Overcome' features Sanders reciting folk classics over backing musicians; it resurfaced gloriously during his presidential runs.

questions.q: As mayor, Sanders established a sister-city relationship between Burlington and Puerto Cabezas, a city in which country?
questions.explanation: The 1984 pairing with Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua was a Cold War statement; Burlington also linked with Yaroslavl in the USSR in 1988.

questions.q: Before becoming mayor, Bernie Sanders ran repeatedly (and badly) for statewide office under the banner of which Vermont third party?
questions.explanation: Sanders ran for Senate and governor in the 1970s as a Liberty Union candidate, never topping 6%.

questions.q: Sanders' mayoral wing of Burlington politics grew into which party, still a force on the city council?
questions.explanation: The 'Sanderistas' became the Progressive Coalition, then the Vermont Progressive Party — among America's most successful third parties.

questions.q: When Bernie Sanders won Vermont's U.S. House seat in 1990, he became the first what in 40 years?
questions.explanation: Sanders was the first independent elected to the House in four decades; he moved to the Senate in 2007.

questions.q: Which Vermont senator served longer than anyone else in the state's history and appeared in five Batman films?
questions.explanation: Patrick Leahy (1975–2023) was a lifelong Batman fan whose cameos included getting throttled by Heath Ledger's Joker in 'The Dark Knight.'

questions.q: In 2001, which Vermont senator's departure from the Republican Party flipped control of the U.S. Senate?
questions.explanation: Jim Jeffords became an independent caucusing with Democrats in May 2001, handing them the Senate majority — a political earthquake.

questions.q: Who was Vermont's first female governor, elected in 1984?
questions.explanation: Madeleine Kunin served three terms (1985–1991) and was the first Jewish woman elected governor of any state.

questions.q: Which Vermont governor's 2004 presidential campaign ended with a famous 'scream' in Iowa?
questions.explanation: Howard Dean, governor 1991–2003, pioneered internet fundraising before the 'Dean Scream' punctured his campaign.

questions.q: Vermont was the last state to elect a woman to Congress. Who finally broke the streak in 2022?
questions.explanation: Becca Balint's 2022 House win made Vermont the 50th and final state to send a woman to Congress.

questions.q: How many seats does Vermont have in the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: Vermont's small population earns it a single at-large House seat.

questions.q: Town Meeting Day, when Vermonters gather to vote on local budgets in person, falls on which day?
questions.explanation: Town Meeting Day, a legal state holiday, keeps direct democracy alive on the first Tuesday of March.

questions.q: Vermont's two official state holidays unique to it are Town Meeting Day and what August observance?
questions.explanation: Bennington Battle Day (August 16) commemorates the 1777 Revolutionary victory.

questions.q: What is unusual about how Vermont's governor is elected if no candidate wins a majority?
choices: The secretary of state decides by lot
The plurality winner takes office automatically
questions.explanation: Vermont's constitution sends gubernatorial races to the General Assembly if no one clears 50% — it has happened more than 20 times.

questions.q: Vermont governors serve terms of what length — the shortest in the nation, shared only with New Hampshire?
questions.explanation: Vermont and New Hampshire are the only states with two-year gubernatorial terms.

questions.q: Which crusty Republican senator from Putney famously advised that the U.S. should 'declare victory and get out' of Vietnam?
questions.explanation: George Aiken, senator 1941–1975, was credited with the 'declare victory' formula (his actual words were subtler) and spent famously little on campaigns.

questions.q: Which Vermont senator delivered a landmark 1954 speech condemning Joseph McCarthy, comparing his tactics to 'a new party… dedicated to fear'?
questions.explanation: Ralph Flanders introduced the censure resolution against McCarthy that the Senate passed in December 1954.

questions.q: Vermont voted for the losing candidate in every presidential election from 1856 to 1988 except twice — it was one of only two states to vote against FDR all four times. Which party did it back that whole century?
questions.explanation: Rock-ribbed Republican Vermont went GOP in every presidential race from 1856 until LBJ carried it in 1964; with Maine, it resisted all four FDR landslides.

questions.q: Since 1992, Vermont has voted for president how?
questions.explanation: Once the most Republican state, Vermont has gone Democratic in every presidential election since 1992 — one of the great partisan flips.

questions.q: Vermont's first-in-the-nation 2014 law attempted (unsuccessfully at first) to create what statewide?
questions.explanation: Green Mountain Care would have been America's first single-payer system; Governor Shumlin shelved it over financing in December 2014.

questions.q: Who became Burlington's first female mayor when she took office in 2024?
questions.explanation: Progressive Emma Mulvaney-Stanak won in March 2024, succeeding Miro Weinberger and becoming the city's first woman and first openly LGBTQ mayor.

questions.q: Miro Weinberger, Burlington's mayor from 2012 to 2024, belonged to which party — the first of that party to hold the office in decades?
questions.explanation: Weinberger's 2012 win returned the mayor's office to Democrats for the first time since 1981, after Sanders-era Progressives and others held it.

questions.q: Vermont's legislature is called what?
choices: The Vermont Great and General Court
questions.explanation: The General Assembly comprises a 150-member House and 30-member Senate, meeting in Montpelier's gold-domed State House.

questions.q: What tops the golden dome of the Vermont State House?
choices: A statue of Ceres, goddess of agriculture
questions.explanation: A 14-foot statue of Ceres crowns the dome; the current carving was installed in 2018, the third since 1858.

questions.q: Vermont's official state motto is what?
questions.explanation: 'Freedom and Unity' has been on the state seal since 1779; 'Stella quarta decima fulgeat' (may the 14th star shine bright) became the Latin motto in 2015.

questions.q: In 2015, Vermont adopted an official Latin motto: 'Stella quarta decima fulgeat.' What does it mean?
questions.explanation: Proposed by a Latin student, it honors Vermont as the 14th state; some confused commenters thought the state was adopting 'Latin American' language.

questions.q: Vermont is one of only two states that allow what at the ballot box for governor?
choices: It's one of two with two-year gubernatorial terms
questions.explanation: Only Vermont and New Hampshire still elect governors every two years.

questions.q: Burlington voters legalized what in a much-watched 2014 charter-change era debate over the lakefront?
choices: Redevelopment of the Moran Plant (ultimately unbuilt)
questions.explanation: Voters backed the 'New Moran' plan in 2014; when it stalled, the plant was stripped to its steel frame — today's FRAME overlook.

questions.q: What did Vermont do first in the nation on July 1, 2018, via legislature rather than ballot initiative?
questions.explanation: Vermont was the first state to legalize recreational marijuana possession through its legislature rather than a referendum.

questions.q: Which Vermont senator became the first U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations?
questions.explanation: Warren Austin of Highgate and Burlington served as the first U.S. Ambassador to the UN from 1947 to 1953.

questions.q: Burlington City Hall and its park anchor the south end of Church Street. Who designed the 1928 building, of Vermont brick, marble, and granite?
questions.explanation: The famed firm McKim, Mead & White designed Burlington City Hall — partner William Mead was a Vermonter, born in Brattleboro.

questions.q: Vermont's U.S. Senate delegation since 2007 — Leahy/Welch and Sanders — has been notable for what?
choices: Being the oldest pair in Senate history
Both members being born in Brooklyn
questions.explanation: Bernie Sanders is the longest-serving independent in congressional history (Peter Welch took Leahy's seat in 2023).

questions.q: Where was Bernie Sanders born?
questions.explanation: Sanders grew up in Flatbush, Brooklyn and moved to Vermont in 1968 — the accent never left.

questions.q: The mitten-clad Bernie Sanders meme photo of January 2021 was taken at what event?
questions.explanation: Bundled in a Burton jacket and Vermont-made wool mittens at the inauguration, Bernie became a global meme; the mittens were made by a Vermont teacher.

questions.q: As mayor, Bernie Sanders fought to keep Burlington's waterfront from becoming what?
questions.explanation: Sanders opposed the Alden Plan's private development, pushing the 'people's waterfront' of parks, the bike path, and public access that exists today.

questions.q: Vermont's current governor as of 2026, a Republican first elected in 2016, is who?
questions.explanation: Phil Scott, a former stock-car racer and construction executive from Berlin, VT, has won repeated terms in deep-blue Vermont.

questions.q: Governor Phil Scott is known for what hobby, unusual among governors?
choices: Stock car racing at Thunder Road
questions.explanation: Scott has raced (and won) for decades at Thunder Road Speedbowl in Barre.

questions.q: What is a 'side judge' in Vermont?
choices: An elected lay judge who sits alongside the presiding judge in county court
questions.explanation: Vermont's elected assistant judges — 'side judges' — are a colonial-era institution nearly unique to the state.

questions.q: Burlington's minor-league baseball team, playing at Centennial Field, is called what?
questions.explanation: The Lake Monsters — named for Champ, who is also the mascot — have played at Centennial Field since 1994 (as the Expos until 2006).

questions.q: Centennial Field, home of the Lake Monsters, first hosted baseball in what year — making it one of America's oldest ballparks?
questions.explanation: Built for UVM's centennial class, Centennial Field opened in 1906 and its 1922 grandstand still stands.

questions.q: In 2021 the Lake Monsters left affiliated baseball and joined which league?
questions.explanation: After MLB's minor-league contraction, the Lake Monsters became a summer collegiate team in the FCBL — and won the 2021 title.

questions.q: Vermont Green FC, the wildly popular soccer club founded in 2022, plays home games where?
questions.explanation: The environmental-justice-themed USL League Two club packs Virtue Field on UVM's campus and won the 2025 national championship.

questions.q: Which St. Albans-born winger became the first Vermonter to score 50 goals in an NHL season?
questions.explanation: John LeClair, of UVM and the Flyers' 'Legion of Doom' line, notched three straight 50-goal seasons in the 1990s.

questions.q: Which future Hockey Hall of Famer starred at UVM from 1993 to 1997 before winning a Stanley Cup and MVP with Tampa Bay?
questions.explanation: Martin St. Louis, with linemate Éric Perrin and goalie Tim Thomas, made the mid-90s a golden era at the Gut before his Hall of Fame NHL career.

questions.q: UVM basketball's greatest upset came in the 2005 NCAA tournament, when Taylor Coppenrath, T.J. Sorrentine, and coach Tom Brennan's Catamounts knocked off which powerhouse?
questions.explanation: 13-seed Vermont beat 4-seed Syracuse in overtime; Sorrentine's shot 'from the parking lot' is Vermont sports scripture.

questions.q: Snowboarding pioneer Jake Burton Carpenter founded Burton Snowboards in Vermont in what year?
questions.explanation: Burton started shaping boards in a Londonderry barn in 1977; the company's headquarters is in Burlington.

questions.q: Which Vermont ski area, opened in 1948, still runs America's only single-chair lift and sells the bumper sticker 'Ski It If You Can'?
questions.explanation: Mad River Glen in Fayston is also the only major U.S. ski area owned by a skiers' cooperative — and it still bans snowboards.

questions.q: Mad River Glen is one of only three U.S. ski areas that ban what?
questions.explanation: Alongside Alta and Deer Valley in Utah, Mad River Glen remains skiers-only.

questions.q: Which resort bills itself as the 'Ski Capital of the East' at the foot of Mount Mansfield?
questions.explanation: Stowe Mountain Resort has traded on the title since the 1930s, when CCC crews cut its first trails.

questions.q: Killington's nickname reflects its size. What is it?
questions.explanation: Killington, the largest ski area in the eastern U.S., has been 'The Beast' for decades and hosts World Cup races each November.

questions.q: Jay Peak, near the Canadian border, is famous among skiers for what?
choices: The steepest lift-served run in the U.S.
Getting the most snow in eastern North America
questions.explanation: The 'Jay Cloud' delivers the East's biggest snow totals — averaging around 350 inches a year.

questions.q: The Jay Peak resort was at the center of what scandal, the biggest fraud case in Vermont history?
choices: An EB-5 investor visa Ponzi-like scheme
questions.explanation: Owners misused over $200 million in EB-5 immigrant-investor funds; the SEC seized the resort in 2016 and owner Ariel Quiros went to prison.

questions.q: Which Vermonter won two gold medals in alpine skiing at the 1952 Olympics, still a benchmark for American ski racing?
questions.explanation: Andrea Mead Lawrence of Rutland (whose family founded Pico) won slalom and giant slalom at Oslo at age 19.

questions.q: The 'Skiing Cochrans' run a legendary backyard-scale ski area in which town outside Burlington?
questions.explanation: Cochran's Ski Area in Richmond has produced generations of Olympians, from 1972 slalom gold medalist Barbara Ann Cochran to her son Ryan Cochran-Siegle, 2022 super-G silver medalist.

questions.q: Bill Koch of Guilford, Vermont made Olympic history in 1976 as the first American to win a medal in which sport?
questions.explanation: Koch's silver at Innsbruck remains a landmark; he later popularized the skating technique. The Catamount Trail's youth program bears his name.

questions.q: Snowboarder Ross Powers, who won halfpipe gold at the 2002 Olympics, grew up riding at which southern Vermont mountain?
questions.explanation: Powers, from Londonderry, learned at Bromley and trained at Stratton — part of Vermont's remarkable snowboard-medal pipeline.

questions.q: Which Belmont, Vermont native won snowboard halfpipe gold at Torino 2006 and bronze at Vancouver 2010 — and has a maple syrup brand?
questions.explanation: Hannah Teter's 'Hannah's Gold' syrup funds charity; fellow Vermont-trained rider Kelly Clark (West Dover) won gold in 2002.

questions.q: Golfer Keegan Bradley, who won the 2011 PGA Championship and captained the 2025 U.S. Ryder Cup team, hails from which Vermont town?
questions.explanation: Bradley grew up in Woodstock; his aunt is LPGA Hall of Famer Pat Bradley.

questions.q: The Vermont City Marathon runs through Burlington on Memorial Day weekend, finishing where?
questions.explanation: The KeyBank Vermont City Marathon, run since 1989, finishes on the lake at Waterfront Park.

questions.q: What is the Catamount Trail?
choices: A 300-mile backcountry ski trail running the length of Vermont
questions.explanation: The Catamount Trail is the longest backcountry ski trail in North America, paralleling the Long Trail's spirit in winter.

questions.q: Kingdom Trails, ranked among the best mountain-bike networks in North America, spreads out from which NEK village?
questions.explanation: Over 100 miles of flowy singletrack on private land made East Burke a mountain-biking mecca.

questions.q: What are Vermont's official state sports?
questions.explanation: Vermont recognizes both skiing and snowboarding as its official state sports — fitting for the state that produced Burton.

questions.q: Thunder Road Speedbowl, 'the nation's site of excitement,' hosts stock car racing in which granite city?
questions.explanation: The quarter-mile high-banked oval in Barre has run since 1960; Governor Phil Scott has raced there for decades.

questions.q: 'In Search of Memphre,' one of Vermont's boldest open-water swims, crosses 25 miles of Lake Memphremagog from Newport to which country?
choices: The United States (it stays in Vermont)
questions.explanation: Kingdom Games' marathon swim runs the length of Memphremagog across the international border to Magog, Quebec.

questions.q: UVM's men's soccer team won its first national title in 2024. In which division?
questions.explanation: The Catamounts won the 2024 College Cup — Vermont's first Division I men's soccer national championship, and the school's first D-I team title.

questions.q: UVM men's basketball has dominated which conference, winning its regular-season title year after year?
questions.explanation: The Catamounts have been the powerhouse of the America East Conference for two decades, making regular NCAA tournament trips.

questions.q: The Penguin Plunge each February sends costumed Vermonters into Lake Champlain to benefit which organization?
questions.explanation: The Burlington Penguin Plunge at Waterfront Park is Special Olympics Vermont's biggest fundraiser.

questions.q: What annual winter event turns Lake Champlain's broad ice into a fishing festival centered on which tasty native fish?
questions.explanation: Ice-fishing derbies for yellow perch and smelt are a Champlain winter tradition when the ice allows.

questions.q: Lake Champlain is renowned among anglers as one of America's best fisheries for which sport fish?
questions.explanation: Champlain regularly hosts Bassmaster and MLF tournaments thanks to its outstanding bass fishery.

questions.q: The Green Mountain Club, founded in 1910, exists primarily to maintain what?
choices: The Appalachian Trail in New Hampshire
questions.explanation: The GMC built and still maintains the 272-mile Long Trail and its 70 backcountry shelters.

questions.q: Vermonter Ryan Cochran-Siegle won Olympic silver in 2022 in which event?
questions.explanation: Cochran-Siegle of the Richmond skiing Cochrans took super-G silver in Beijing, 50 years after his mother Barbara Ann's slalom gold.

questions.q: The 10th Mountain Division, the U.S. Army's famed WWII ski troops, was championed by Minnie Dole — founder of what organization with deep Stowe roots?
questions.explanation: Charles Minot 'Minnie' Dole founded the National Ski Patrol in 1938 after ski accidents in the Mansfield region, then lobbied the Army to create mountain troops.

questions.q: North Beach, Burlington's sandy summer hangout, sits at the edge of which neighborhood?
questions.explanation: North Beach and its campground line the lake below North Avenue in the New North End.

questions.q: Oakledge Park in Burlington's South End is home to Vermont's first what?
questions.explanation: Oakledge's wheelchair-accessible treehouse opened in 2007; the park's lakeside ledges are also a classic sunset perch.

questions.q: The Burlington Bike Path, backbone of lakeside recreation, follows the bed of which former railroad?
questions.explanation: The 8-mile path follows the old Rutland Railroad Island Line along the lake, continuing onto the Colchester causeway.

questions.q: How long is the Long Trail, end to end?
questions.explanation: The Long Trail runs roughly 272 miles from the Massachusetts border to Canada along the Green Mountain spine.

questions.q: What is the hottest temperature ever recorded in Burlington?
questions.explanation: Burlington hit 101°F on August 11, 1944 — still the city's all-time record.

questions.q: Burlington's biggest single snowstorm dumped 33.1 inches in early January of which year?
questions.explanation: The January 2–3, 2010 storm buried Burlington under a record 33.1 inches of featherweight powder.

questions.q: About how much snow does Burlington get in an average winter?
questions.explanation: Burlington averages roughly 80 inches of snow a season — while Jay Peak's summit can see over 300.

questions.q: Vermont's all-time coldest temperature, -50°F, was recorded in 1933 in which Northeast Kingdom town?
questions.explanation: Bloomfield's -50°F on December 30, 1933 ties the coldest reading ever recorded in New England.

questions.q: Vermont's all-time hottest temperature, 105°F, was set on July 4, 1911 in which Connecticut River town?
questions.explanation: Vernon, in Vermont's southeast corner, hit 105°F during the deadly July 1911 heat wave.

questions.q: The Great Flood of 1927, Vermont's deadliest natural disaster, killed 84 people including which state official?
questions.explanation: Lt. Gov. S. Hollister Jackson drowned near his Barre home when the November 3–4, 1927 flood devastated the state.

questions.q: Tropical Storm Irene ravaged Vermont in August of which year, washing out 500+ miles of road?
questions.explanation: Irene's August 28, 2011 deluge isolated 13 towns, destroyed historic covered bridges, and became a defining Vermont disaster.

questions.q: In July 2023 (and again in 2024), Vermont suffered catastrophic flooding that put which city's downtown underwater?
questions.explanation: The July 2023 floods filled Montpelier's downtown with feet of water, drawing comparisons to 1927 and Irene.

questions.q: The January 1998 disaster that left much of northern Vermont dark for days was what?
questions.explanation: The Great Ice Storm of January 1998 coated the region in up to three inches of ice, snapping trees and power lines across Vermont, New York, and Quebec.

questions.q: On average, Lake Champlain's 'broad lake' freezes completely over how often in recent decades?
choices: Only in a minority of winters — it's become rare
questions.explanation: The lake once closed most winters; warming has made a full freeze-over the exception since the 1990s.

questions.q: What lake-driven weather quirk keeps Burlington's shoreline slightly milder than inland Vermont?
choices: The lake's stored heat moderates temperatures
questions.explanation: Lake Champlain's thermal mass takes the edge off early-winter cold and cools lakeside summer days — Burlington's own micro-climate.

questions.q: Vermont's state bird is which famously musical forest dweller?
questions.explanation: The hermit thrush, with its flute-like song, has been the state bird since 1941.

questions.q: What is Vermont's state flower?
questions.explanation: Red clover, a staple of dairy pastures, became the state flower in 1894.

questions.q: Vermont's state tree — no surprise — is what?
questions.explanation: The sugar maple, source of all that syrup and October color, was designated in 1949.

questions.q: Vermont's state animal is which homegrown breed?
questions.explanation: Every Morgan horse descends from Justin Morgan's stallion Figure, foaled in the 1790s and raised in Randolph, Vermont.

questions.q: Vermont's official state fossil is what?
choices: A trilobite from Isle La Motte
A beluga whale skeleton found in Charlotte
questions.explanation: The 11,000-year-old 'Charlotte whale,' dug up by railroad workers in 1849, proved an arm of the sea once covered the Champlain Valley.

questions.q: How did a whale skeleton end up buried in Charlotte, Vermont, 150 miles from the ocean?
choices: Lake Champlain connects to the ocean underground
The Champlain Sea, a post-glacial arm of the Atlantic, once covered the valley
Settlers hauled it for whale oil
questions.explanation: After the glaciers retreated ~12,000 years ago, seawater flooded the depressed land, creating the Champlain Sea — home to belugas.

questions.q: Vermont's state insect is what?
questions.explanation: The honeybee has been Vermont's state insect since 1978.

questions.q: Vermont designates three state rocks. Which trio is it?
questions.explanation: The three pillars of Vermont's quarrying history — marble (Rutland County), granite (Barre), slate (the western border) — share the honor.
